A third view explains the threshold as orig. “a threshing-floor, because in ancient times the floor at the entrance was used for threshing” (Cleasby and Vigfusson); but the threshing could not have been accomplished on the narrow sills which form thresholds, and it was only in comparatively few houses that threshing was done at all.] '''1.''' The plank, stone, or piece of timber which lies at the bottom of a door, or under it, particularly the door of a dwelling-house, church, temple, or other building; a door-sill; hence, entrance; gate; door. {{smaller block|Ther with the nyghtspel seyde he anon rightes
On foure halves of the hous aboute,
And on the ''thresshfold'' of the dore withoute. {{right|''Chaucer'', Miller's Tale, l. 296.}} Still at hell's dark ''threshold'' to have sat watch. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 594.}} Forward leaped she o'er the ''threshold'',
Eager as a glancing surf. ''Lowell'', The Captive.}} '''2.''' Hence, the place or point of entering or beginning; outset: as, he is now at the ''threshold'' of his argument. {{smaller block|The fair new forms
That float about the ''threshold'' of an age,
Like truths of Science waiting to be caught. {{right|''Tennyson'', Golden Year.}}}} '''3.''' In ''psychol.'', the limit below which a given stimulus, or the difference between two stimuli, ceases to be perceptible. Compare ''schwelle''.—'''Dweller on the threshold.''' {{smaller|See ''dweller''.}}—'''Stimulus threshold.''' {{smaller|See ''stimulus''.}} '''threshwold†, thresshfold†,''' ''n.'' N. D., i. 1. 74.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thrice'' he assay'd, and ''thrice'', in spite of scorn,
Tears such as angels weep burst forth. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 619.}}}} 2. Hence, in a general sense, repeatedly; emphatically; fully. {{smaller block|''Thrice'' is he armed that hath his quarrel just. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. [A var. of ''thread'' through the form ''threed'', the long ''ee'' being shortened as in ''breeches'', ''threepence'', ''been'', etc.] Same as ''thread''. {{smaller block|And make his bridle a bottom of ''thrid'',
To roll up how many miles you have rid. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Masque of Queens.}}}} '''thrid'''1 (thrid), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''thridded'', ppr. ''thridding''. Same as ''thread''. [Obsolete or archaic.] {{smaller block|Uncle, good uncle, see! the thin starv'd rascal,

''thrift'', < Icel. ''thrift'' (= Sw. Dan. ''drift''), thrift, < ''thrīfa'' (refl. ''thrīfask''), thrive: see ''thrive''.] 1†. The condition of one who thrives; luck; fortune; success; prosperity. {{smaller block|"Goode ''thrift'' have ye," quod Eleyne the queene. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1687.}}}} {{smaller block|No, let the candied tongue lick absurd pomp, And crook the pregnant hinges of the knee Where ''thrift'' may follow fawning. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 67.}}}} 2. Frugality; economical management; economy; good husbandry. {{smaller block|The rest, . . . willing to fall to ''thrift'', prove very good husbands. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} {{smaller block|It is one degree of ''thrift'' . . . to bring our debts into as few hands as we can. {{right|''Donne'', Sermons, ix.}}}} 3. [A particular use, with ref. to vigorous growth.] A plant of the genus ''Armeria'', of the order ''Plumbagineæ'', a genus much resembling ''Statice'', the marsh-rosemary, except that the flowers are gathered into globular heads. {{smaller|The common thrift is ''A. vulgaris'' (''A. maritima''), a plant abounding on the shores, also in the mountains, of the northern Old World, found also on the western coast of North America, and appearing again in the southern hemisphere beyond the tropics. It grows in tufts of several leafless stalks from a rosette of many narrow radical leaves. The flowers are pink or sometimes white, disposed in dense heads. The plant is often cultivated for borders. Old or local names are ''lady's-cushion'', ''sea-pink'', ''sea-thrift'', and ''sea-gillyflower''. The plantain-leaved thrift is ''A. plantaginea'', like the former, but with much broader leaves. The great thrift, ''A. latifolia'' (''A. cephalotes''), of the Mediterranean region, is highly recommended for gardens, but is somewhat tender. Their slender household fortunes (for the man
Had risk'd his little), like the little ''thrift'',
Trembled in perilous places o'er a deep. {{right|''Tennyson'', Sea Dreams.}}}} 4. Same as ''thrift-box''.—{{smaller|'''Lavender thrift''', a name for species of ''Statice'', especially ''S. Limonium''.—'''Prickly thrift''', a plant of the genus ''Acantholimon'', of the ''Plumbagineæ'', of which some species, as ''A. glumaceum'', are choice border-plants.—'''To bid good thrift†''', to wish well to; congratulate. ''Chaucer''.=Syn. 2. ''Frugality'', etc. See ''economy''.}} '''thrift-box''' (thrift′boks), ''n.'' A small box for keeping savings; a money-box. Also called ''apprentice-box''. '''thriftily''' (thrif′ti-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thriftily''; < ''thrifty'' + ''-ly''2.] 1. In a thrifty manner; frugally; carefully; with the carefulness and prudence which characterize good husbandry; economically. {{smaller block|Hee hurd tell of a towne ''thriftily'' walled,
A citie sett by peece with full siker wardes. {{right|''Alisaunder of Macedoine'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1206.}}}} 2†. Punctiliously; politely. {{smaller block|A yong clerk romynge by hymself they mette,
Which that in Latin ''thriftily'' hem grette. {{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin's Tale, l. 446.}}}} '''thriftiness''' (thrif′ti-nes), ''n.'' [< ''thrifty'' + ''-ness''.] The character of being thrifty; frugality; good husbandry. {{smaller block|Indeed I wonder'd that your wary ''thriftiness'',
Not wont to drop one penny in a quarter
Idly, would part with such a sum so easily. {{right|''Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, iii. 1.}}}} '''thriftless''' (thrift′les), ''a.'' [< ''thrift'' + ''-less''.] 1. Having no thrift, frugality, or good management; profuse; extravagant. {{smaller block|He shall spend mine honour with his shame,
As ''thriftless'' sons their scraping fathers' gold. {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 3. 69.}}}} {{smaller block|She had a vocation to hold in check his ''thriftless'' propensities. {{right|''E. Eggleston'', The Graysons, xxiv.}}}} 2†. Producing no gain; unprofitable. {{smaller block|What ''thriftless'' sighs shall poor Olivia breathe! {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 2. 40.}}}} '''thriftlessly''' (thrift′les-li), ''adv.'' [< ''thriftless'' + ''-ly''2.] In a thriftless manner; extravagantly. '''thriftlessness''' (thrift′les-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being thriftless. '''thrifty''' (thrif′ti), ''a.'' [< ME. ''thrifty'' (= Sw. Dan. ''driftig''); < ''thrift'' + ''-y''1.] 1. Characterized by thrift; frugal; sparing; careful; economical; saving; using economy and good management. {{smaller block|Thou dost impudently to make a ''thrifty'' purchase of boldnesse to thy selfe out of the painfull merits of other men. {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii., Int.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thrifty'' housewives and industrious spinsters. {{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 173.}}}} 2. Thriving; flourishing; successful; prosperous; fortunate. {{smaller block|He is as wys, discret, and as secree
As any man I woot of his degree,
And therto manly and eek servisable,
And for to been a ''thrifty'' man right able. {{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant's Tale, l. 668.}}}} {{smaller block|The houses were large and comfortable, and the people had a ''thrifty'', prosperous, and satisfied air. {{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 44.}}}} 3†. Well-husbanded. {{smaller block|I have five hundred crowns,
The ''thrifty'' hire I saved under your father. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 3. 39.}} Keep them from wronging others, or neglect Of duty in themselves; correct the blood With ''thrifty'' bits and labour. {{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, v. 5.}}}} '''4†.''' Showing marks of thrift; expensive; rich. {{smaller block|Why is my neighebores wyf so gay? She is honoured over al ther she gooth; I sitte at hoom, I have no ''thrifty'' clooth. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath's Tale, l. 238.}}}} '''5†.''' Useful; profitable. {{smaller block|Good men, herkeneth everich on, This was a ''thrifty'' tale for the nones. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Shipman's Tale, l. 3.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' See ''economy''.}} '''thrill1''' (thril), ''v.'' [< ME. ''thrillen'', ''thryllen'', a transposed form of ''thirlen'', ''thyrlen'', E. ''thirl'': see ''thirl''1. Cf. ''trill''1, ''drill''1.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To bore; pierce; perforate; drill; thirl. Compare ''thirl''1, 1. {{smaller block|He cowde his comyng not forbere, Though ye him ''thrilled'' with a spere. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 7634.}}}} '''2.''' To penetrate or permeate with a sudden wave of feeling, as of pleasure, pity, remorse, etc.; affect or fill with a tingling emotion or sensation. Compare ''thirl''1, 2. {{smaller block|A servant that he bred, ''thrill'd'' with remorse, Opposed against the act. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 2. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|How calm a moment may precede One that shall ''thrill'' the world forever! {{right|''A. Dommett'', Christmas Hymn.}}}} {{smaller block|His deep voice ''thrilled'' the awe-struck, listening folk. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 415.}}}}
